dropped_claims.claim: The National Museum of Nuclear Science & History, through its Atomic Heritage Foundation site, preserves a documented account of the radium dial painters' story, including Grace Fryer's lawsuit.

claims.claim: Dial painters at the United States Radium Corporation were encouraged to point their brushes with their lips, with no safety precautions taken.
claims.episode_span: Supervisors had shown the young women how to keep a fine point on each brush by drawing the bristles between their lips
claims.source_title: The Radium Girls - Nuclear Museum (Atomic Heritage Foundation)
claims.supporting_quote: No safety precautions were taken, and the women were even encouraged to lick their brushes to keep the tip pointed and prevent the paint from drying.

claims.claim: USRC supervisors taught workers the 'lip, dip, paint' technique because brushes lost their shape after a few strokes.
claims.episode_span: The work required steady hands and speed, so foremen taught the “lip-pointing” method as standard practice.
claims.supporting_quote: The brushes would lose shape after a few strokes, so the USRC supervisors encouraged their workers to shape the brushes' point with their lips ("lip, dip, paint") or use their tongues to keep them sharp.

claims.claim: Grace Fryer sued US Radium together with four other dial painters — Edna Hussman, Katherine Schaub, Quinta McDonald, and Albina Larice.
claims.episode_span: Grace Fryer and four colleagues filed suit in 1927 after learning their conditions were linked to the paint.
claims.supporting_quote: The five factory workers involved in the suit were dubbed "the Radium Girls" – Fryer, Edna Hussman, Katherine Schaub, Quinta McDonald, and Albina Larice.

claims.claim: The Radium Girls' case against USRC was settled in the autumn of 1928, before the jury deliberated.
claims.episode_span: The five plaintiffs received modest settlements in 1928
claims.supporting_quote: USRC denied any wrongdoing, but the case was settled in the autumn of 1928 before the trial was deliberated by the jury.

claims.claim: The settlement gave each of the five women $10,000 plus a $600 annual payment.
claims.episode_span: The five plaintiffs received modest settlements in 1928, but by then at least 30 former dial painters had died
claims.source_title: The Radium Girls - Nuclear Museum (Atomic Heritage Foundation)
claims.supporting_quote: In desperate need of money, they would eventually settle for $10,000 each and a $600 annual payment, although none of them would survive more than two years after the settlement.

claims.claim: Harvard physiologist Cecil Drinker investigated the US Radium factory and reported pervasive radium contamination of the workroom and the workers.
claims.episode_span: management had received warnings from a Harvard physiologist in 1924 yet continued the lip-pointing instruction
claims.source_title: The Radium Girls - Nuclear Museum (Atomic Heritage Foundation)
claims.supporting_quote: Harvard physiologist Cecil Drinker, who later investigated the factories, reported , “Dust samples collected in the workroom from various locations and from chairs not used by the workers were all luminous in the dark room.

claims.claim: The former US Radium plant site in Orange, New Jersey is an EPA Superfund site.
claims.episode_span: Today the former Orange plant site is a Superfund location
claims.source_title: U.S. RADIUM CORP. | Superfund Site Profile | US EPA
claims.supporting_quote: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conducted its fourth Five-Year Review (FYR) of the U.S. Radium Superfund site, located in Orange, New Jersey.

claims.claim: US Radium held World War I government contracts to produce luminous watches and airplane instruments for American soldiers.
claims.episode_span: military planners needed reliable luminous markings on aircraft instruments, ship compasses, and trench watches
claims.source_title: The Radium Girls - Nuclear Museum (Atomic Heritage Foundation)
claims.supporting_quote: U.S. Radium would also receive government contracts during World War I to produce watches and airplane instruments for American soldiers.
